Connectivity

Settlements are considered connected if they are linked with a direct road (intermediate roads that run through other Settlements do not count) or if they are both coastal Settlements on the same continent.
Restrictions

[BLIST][LI]Unrest: Towns cannot start a project while in Unrest. After capturing a settlement, Civs must wait until the unrest period is over before assigning a Town a specialization.[LI]Permanent Specialization: Once a Town’s Focus is selected, it is locked in permanently. Choose wisely![/LIST]
Buildings and Specialists
Growing Towns can only purchase Warehouse Buildings without further specializations.
Upgrading to a City
Towns can be converted into Cities, but this costs Gold and the loss of the Town Focus and Growth bonuses upon conversion. The more population a Town has, the cheaper it is to upgrade to a City.
However, the more Cities you already own, the more expensive your next upgrade will be.

[BLIST][LI]Cost Limits: The upgrade cost has a maximum cap and scales with each City converted. However, Certain Unique Abilities (UA) and other factors can reduce or increase the cost of conversion.[LI]Captured Settlements: Captured Settlements cost double to upgrade, but this charge cannot exceed the Gold cap.[/LIST]
Tip: Instead of converting all Towns into Cities, aim to keep at least a 1 to 1 Town to City ratio.
Production: Yield

Production is one of the main resources in Civilization VII. It is the measure by which Cities build units, buildings, Wonders, and complete projects. As such, Production is as important for City growth as Food, since it determines the speed with which any City erects new structures. However, unlike Food, Production cannot be transported from Towns to Cities, making Production arguably more important; even Cities with large populations cannot produce anything without Production.
Tip: Since Towns do not have a production queue, their production is converted to Gold.
Food: Yield

Settlements require food to grow their population. After Citizens are born, they no longer consume food, but the threshold for the next growth event increases. However, Citizens who become Specialists cost Food to maintain.
Tip: When a Settlement runs out of space to grow, the excess food is used to spawn Migrants.
Growth Moment
Settlements gain control of new tiles by accumulating Food until they reach a threshold. After crossing this threshold, the Settlement gains a Population that can allocate to a tile for growth.
Border Growth

[BLIST][LI]Expansion: Borders expand when a population is placed on a new tile near a Settlement’s border.[LI]Construction: Borders also grow when a building on the border is completed (repairs do not expand the border).[LI]Limitations: A border’s maximum reach is three tiles from its City Center, not counting the center tile itself. Borders cannot overlap with those of other settlements.[LI]Tile Acquisition: When placing a new population or completing a building, the settlement acquires all adjacent tiles, provided this does not conflict with the rule that borders cannot overlap.[/LIST]
Adding Population

[BLIST][LI]Food Accumulation: Food from each Settlement is added to a bucket each turn. Upon crossing the growth threshold, the Settlement gains a Population.[LI]Population Allocation: Players can choose between placing a new Population on an empty tile for an Improvement or adding it to an Urban tile to gain a Specialist.[LI]Growth Rate: Modifiers that use this term are effects that decrease the amount of Food a Settlement needs to grow a Population.[/LIST]
Tip: Food is the primary driver of population growth. Increase a City’s food supply by setting a connected Town's focus to send additional food to the City.
Constructibles: Placement

New to Civilization VII, players can now place Constructibles on owned Rural tiles, provided they are connected to an Urban tile or City Center. This action automatically converts the tile into an Urban tile. Two Buildings can typically fit onto a single tile, while Wonders occupy the entire space. However, some buildings, such as Aerodromes, also consume a full tile.
Tip: If a tile is full but contains buildings from a previous Age, you can overbuild the outdated buildings.
Fortifications
A Fortification is any type of structure that increases the defense of the tile. The most common type of Fortification is Walls, but certain Wonders and Improvements can also be Fortifications.

Tip: Military Units can also create temporary Fortifications, which can help a Unit defend the tile more effectively. Build temporary Fortifications where you know combat will take place, or to protect a critical area. Be warned: once temporary Fortifications are abandoned, they will disappear.
Walls
Players can build Walls in Cities or purchase them in both Cities or Towns.

Wall defenses increase a District's health by 100. Walls from the previous Age provide only half the defense bonus and half the District health, while Walls older than one age provide no benefit. However, Walls from the previous Age can be upgraded by overbuilding them with the current age defenses. Walls are not repaired through the City production queue; they automatically repair over time as long as they are not under attack and have no adjacent enemy Units.

Wall defenses cannot be purchased with Gold, except in the City Center. Instead, Walls in Districts can be constructed one tile at a time from the City build queue, using Production. Walls cannot be constructed on Navigable River hexes and must be built adjacent to other Walls from the same Settlement, starting with the City Center. Walls cannot be built adjacent to Walls owned by a different Settlement, except in the City Center, which is always allowed. Walls cannot be constructed on Rural tiles.

When a Unit attacks a defensible District, combat is resolved by taking the attacking Unit's strength and comparing it to the defense strength of the District, which is calculated based on the strongest melee unit trained by the District owner minus a set value (10). Walls and all City or Town Centers deal reciprocal damage to melee attackers, defender first.
Tip: To capture a Settlement, attackers must gain control of the City/Town Center and any Districts with walled defenses.
Settlers
Settlers are essential for expanding an empire.
Settlers can be produced or purchased in any Settlement with at least 5 population. You begin with a Founder that is able to found your Capital City, all subsequent Settlers found Towns.
Tip: Settlers are civilian units and therefore defenseless. It is wise to escort them with a military unit to ensure their safety.
Ages
History is built in layers. No empire has stood the entire test of time. Instead, successor kingdoms build on the glories of their predecessors.

Civilization VII presents each Age as a distinct chapter in human history. Players can either begin each Age by selecting a historical empire and then earn bonuses that can be applied to future Ages. At the beginning of the next Age, players keep the best features of their previous choices as they prepare to explore an enlarged map. The past shapes each Civ, but opportunities to refashion cities and empires means Players are never locked into a specific gameplay path.

Ages harken back to specific times in world history. Cities only contain buildings and wonders that led to the prosperity and civic advancement of the Age. Game systems, such as government, diplomacy, and trade are tailored for each era. Syncretism, a new concept in Civilization VII, also allows the adopting of cultural aspects of an Apex Civilization when playing as a non-Apex Civilization in that Age.

Finally, each Age concludes with a race to put your empire on a pedestal as the greatest kingdom of the era. Players race to build Wonders or to fill their Great Library with all the knowledge of Antiquity and advances toward these objectives provide bonuses for the next Age.
Buildings

Buildings can be constructed through the Production Menu in much the same way units are produced. Some buildings have prerequisites, such as technology or location requirements, and are not visible in the Production Menu until those conditions are met. Additionally, buildings can be purchased in Towns.

When a Building is placed down on a Rural tile, the tile will be converted to an [B]District[/B]. The tile's natural yield will be lost, retaining only the Building's yields. If the tile is occupied by a point of population, that point of population will be refunded, so you can grow again.
[B]It's important to remember that an District has to be placed next to another District, starting with the City Center.[/B]

Non-Warehouse Buildings have scaling costs throughout the game. Their cost increases by 5% for each other non-Warehouse Building in the Settlement, as well as by 10% for each City you have beyond your Capital.

Tip: Some buildings are Ageless, meaning they continue to offer effects regardless of the current Age. Additionally, some buildings have adjacency bonuses, providing extra yields when placed next to specific structures or features.
Buildings: Warehouses

A Warehouse building provides bonuses based on the number of Improvements of the same type within a Settlement. For example, a Granary grants +1 Food for each Farm, Plantation, or Pasture in the settlement. Each of these Improvements provides the same type of bonus: Food. If you have 2 Farms, 1 Plantation, and 1 Pasture, you’d gain +4 Food from building a Granary. The Bonus Yields from Improvements will appear on the Warehouse Buildings they correspond to, rather than on the Improvements themselves.

Tip: Warehouse buildings are Ageless and Buildable in all Ages, which means they survive across Age transitions and can be built in any Age. Warehouses tend to provide huge bonuses to Settlements with a lot of Rural land, but as Urban Districts encroach on Rural, their effectiveness decreases.
Buildings: Standard Buildings

Standard Buildings are the foundational structures available to all civilizations, providing essential yields such as Science, Culture, Production, and more. Unlike Unique Buildings, which are tied to specific civilizations and often come with special bonuses, Standard Buildings are more universally accessible and form the backbone of your infrastructure.

However, as your civilization progresses through different Ages, Standard Buildings undergo changes. During an Age Transition, these buildings lose their adjacency bonuses, retaining only their base yields. This reduction can significantly impact your city's productivity if not addressed.

Despite the loss of adjacency bonuses, Standard Buildings continue to incur maintenance costs. This means they can become economic burdens if not updated or replaced, as they offer diminished returns while still consuming resources.

To mitigate these issues, the game introduces the Overbuilding mechanic. Overbuilding allows you to construct new, more advanced buildings over existing ones, effectively replacing outdated structures with ones that are better suited to the current Age. This process helps restore or even enhance the adjacency bonuses and yields that were lost during the Age Transition.

Regularly assess your cities after each Age Transition. Identify Standard Buildings that have lost their adjacency bonuses and consider overbuilding them with newer structures to maximize efficiency and maintain a strong economy.
Buildings: Unique Buildings

In Civilization VII, some Civs have access to exclusive structures known as Unique Buildings. These Buildings typically offer stronger effects than standard Buildings. When two Unique Buildings from the same Civ are placed on the same tile, they form a Unique Quarter.
Tip: While a Unique Quarter provides substantial benefits, it is not mandatory to place both Unique Buildings on the same tile. Spreading Buildings out can sometimes produce higher yields.
Buildings: Quarters

A Quarter is an Urban District with two non-Wall buildings, where both Buildings are Ageless and/or from the current Age. Full-tile Buildings also count as Quarters. Quarters benefit from various gameplay buffs provided by policies and adjacencies. During a war, all Quarters with Walls or Fortifications must be captured for the settlement to be secured.
Tip: Place two buildings that share adjacency bonuses into the same Quarter and assign Specialists to that tile. The Specialists will provide Yield based on both buildings.
Buildings: Unique Improvements

Unique Improvements are provided by Civ-specific improvements or City-State Suzerain rewards. These must be built through the production queue and overlaid onto regular improvements. However, some placement restrictions apply, and Unique Improvements cannot be built on all improvements. For example, Step Pyramids can only be placed on tiles with a natural Appeal.

Tip: Unique Improvements do not remove yield bonuses from basic improvements, so building them over existing basic improvements is beneficial. However, a Unique Improvement does replace other Unique Improvements on the same tile.
Buildings: Unique Quarter
Players can create a "Unique Quarter" when a Civ has two unique buildings on the same tile. This configuration grants the city a special gameplay bonus, which varies depending on the Civilization.
Tip: Not only do Unique Quarters provide additional bonuses, they also feature unique art, making them visually stunning!
Buildings: Adjacency

Most non-Warehouse Buildings have adjacency bonuses, which provide additional Yield based on the qualities of surrounding tiles. These qualities vary per Building and can include Resources, Terrain, Quarters, Wonders, Improvements, and more. When Specialists are placed on a Building, they provide additional Yield equal to the Building's adjacency bonus. Buildings lose their adjacency bonus when not in their original Age unless they are Ageless.
Tip: Maximize your Yields by placing buildings next to tiles that meet their adjacency requirements, then adding Specialists to further benefit from adjacencies.
Buildings: Ageless

Ageless Buildings will continue to be useful in later Ages. They cannot be overbuilt in later Ages, but their yields, effects, tags, and adjacencies will be retained. Typical Ageless Constructibles include Warehouses, Wonders, Unique Buildings, and Unique Improvements. For example, the Mississippian Potkop is Ageless, so it will always give you its base yield of +1 Gold and +1 Food to Adjacent Resources.
Tip: Despite being permanent, Ageless Buildings are still useful to build. Be considerate of where you place them, and they will help you keep your competitive edge for future Ages.
Buildings: Overbuilding

Most buildings from previous Ages can be overbuilt unless they are tagged as Ageless. This means Players can place a current Age building onto a fully utilized tile as long as that tile contains a qualifying previous Age building. This action removes the lowest yield building on the tile and replaces it with the new building.
Improvements can always be overbuilt with a building.

Tip: Yield bonuses on Quarters and Adjacencies reset with each Age transition. Overbuilding is a valuable strategy to maximize your tile's potential and reintroduce bonus yields back into Quarters and Adjacencies.
Buildings: Maintenance

Most buildings, aside from Warehouse buildings and Wonders, incur maintenance costs in the form of Gold and Happiness. In the Antiquity Age, buildings typically start with a maintenance cost of -2 Gold and -2 Happiness. This cost increases in later Ages, such as -3 Gold and -3 Happiness in the Exploration Age. However, Gold buildings do not have a Gold maintenance cost, and Happiness buildings do not have a Happiness maintenance cost.
Tip: When constructing a lot of buildings, keep a close eye on your Gold and Happiness levels. Building Happiness structures is often essential for maintaining a healthy and expanding empire.
Buildings: Full Tile

Most Buildings only take up half of a District; however, some Buildings need a full District to be built. These full-tile Buildings typically perform critical tasks, like launching rockets or transporting Units via Rail.
Buildings: Water Building

A Water Building is any structure that requires water to be placed. Examples include the Fishing Quay and Wharf. However, buildings that can be placed on water features but don’t actually depend on it, such as a Granary on a minor river, are not considered Water Buildings.
Tip: A general rule of thumb is that if a Building can be placed on Coastal or Navigable River tiles, it’s a Water Building.
Buildings: Military Building

Military Buildings act as spawn points for newly trained Units. For example, once the Barracks has been constructed, newly trained land Units will appear there instead of the City Center. Some bonuses only affect Military Buildings.
Buildings: Built in Line

Some Constructibles, like the Ming Great Wall, can link adjacent copies together to create a line. This line cannot fork or intersect with itself. Constructibles that link together will often give bonuses to adjacent copies.
Buildings: Mill
Mills are Buildings that must be placed on a Minor or Navigable River, such as the Gristmill.
Buildings: Bridge
Land Units may use Bridges to cross a Navigable River on this tile without embarking. Consider building them in convenient locations to keep your Civilization moving.
Projects

Cities can put all their effort and production into a collective goal, or Project, to achieve an outcome that will benefit one’s empire at large. When the many band together, they do what the individual cannot.
Some Projects play an especially important role in the path toward a Science Victory, such as Trans-Oceanic Flight, Break the Sound Barrier, Launch Satellite, and First Crewed Space Flight.
Tip: The Cultural Festival and Research Initiative Projects are available after their study in Antiquity, and from that point onwards can be completed by any City in your empire.
Policies: Basics

Social Policies are a key element of the Culture system in Civilization VII, providing various gameplay effects (buffs) to enhance your civilization. Each Civ has unique versions of these policies, known as "Traditions," which are a special subtype within the Social Policy category.

Key Features of Social Policies:[BLIST][LI]Gameplay Effects: Each Social Policy offers one or more gameplay benefits that can significantly impact your civilization’s performance.[LI]Unlocking: Social Policies are unlocked through the Civics of the Culture Progression tree.[LI]Slotting: These policies are slotted into available Social Policy slots within the Government screen. When new slots are added, Social Policies (and Crisis Policies) can be swapped to optimize your strategy.[LI]Traditions: Traditions, which are the unique Social Policies of each Civ, can be carried forward into the next Age, providing continuity and ongoing benefits as your civilization evolves.[LI]Crisis Policies: During times of Crisis, negative policies may appear, which players are forced to slot, accepting the associated negative consequences.[/LIST]

Common Social Policy effects apply only in the current Age for current Age constructibles and units. Traditions can be slotted and their effect applied in any Age. By strategically managing Social Policies and Traditions and their corresponding slots, players can tailor their civilization's cultural and political strengths to achieve their desired goals.

Tip: Policies must be slotted to be effective. Therefore, increasing your Happiness yield to gain more slots from Celebrations is crucial. A strong Culture strategy relies on robust Happiness management.
Policies: Traditions

Traditions, the unique Social Policies of each Civ, can be carried forward into the next Age, ensuring continuity and ongoing benefits as your Civ evolves. These special policies are marked with a unique icon.
Tip: Invest in Traditions, as they often align with your civilization’s strengths. All of your Traditions will survive into the next Age.
Changing Relationship
Civs have many ways to change their relationship with another Leader. They can initiate or support endeavors with other leaders, which boosts the relationship between both parties.

Alternatively, Players can intentionally lower a relationship by denouncing another Civ. If the relationship worsens sufficiently, Players can declare formal war without using Influence. Conversely, Players can form alliances with leaders if that relationship significantly improves.

Relationships can be influenced in less obvious ways. For example, settling close to another Leader might anger them. Additionally, leaders have Agendas, which can impact their relationships. For instance, having more wonders than Hatshepsut will upset her. You can select a leader's portrait and navigate to the Player info tab to learn about their agenda.

Relationships, positive or negative, will decay over time toward neutral (specifically to a score of 0). The further from neutral the relationship is, the stronger the decay over time will be. This decay is halved with players you are allied or at war with. If you want to keep a specific relationship with a player going, you will need to invest in it!
Tip: If you care about managing relationships, invest in acquiring Influence. Certain buildings, wonders, policies, and towns grant extra Influence.
Befriending Independents

In addition to befriending major Civ leaders, Players can also befriend Independent Powers using a diplomatic action called "Befriend Independent." Once the befriending process is complete, the independent power becomes a [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_SUZERAIN_TOOLTIP]Suzerain[/TIP] [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_CITY_STATE_TOOLTIP]City-State[/TIP], which grants powerful benefits.

Tip: Spending more Influence can speed up the Befriend Independent action. Outpace other players or someone else might claim an Independent Power’s [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_SUZERAIN_TOOLTIP]Suzerain[/TIP] status first. The [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_SUZERAIN_TOOLTIP]Suzerain[/TIP] status is exclusive to one player!
Incite Raid

Incite Raid is a diplomatic action that allows you to direct Independent Powers to launch a raid against another civilization of your choosing. This tactic can be a strategic tool to divert aggression away from your own settlements or to weaken a rival.

To initiate an Incite Raid, locate an Independent Power on the map. Upon interacting with them, you'll have the option to spend Influence to incite a raid. After selecting this option, choose the leader you wish to target. The Independent Power will then prepare to launch a raid against the chosen civilization.

If the targeted Independent Power lacks sufficient military units to conduct the raid, additional units will be spawned to ensure the raid proceeds. This mechanism ensures that the raid can be executed even if the Independent Power is initially under-resourced.

Tip: Use Incite Raid to strategically redirect potential threats away from your empire. By influencing Independent Powers to target rival civilizations, you can create opportunities to strengthen your position or exploit weaknesses in your opponents' defenses.
Trade

Trading requires foreign Settlements to work at least one resource. In the Antiquity Age and the Exploration Age, your Merchant must physically move to a Settlement before being able to establish a Trade Route. Upon establishing a Trade route, you gain GDP and a copy of all the resources in that Settlement, while the other party gains Gold as Trade Income per copy of the resource. Multiple copies of a single resource stack additively, increasing benefits like purchase discounts. Settlements must be part of your trade network to share resources, the range of which is expandable by having a Naval building, properly placed Settlements, and a Town Focus. Reassigning resources is only possible when acquiring new ones or expanding resource slots.
Tip: Accumulate multiple copies of essential resources, such as Gold, to build stacking bonuses that significantly enhance your Gold power.
Trade Range

Land-based trade has a default range between the centers of settlements of 10 tiles in Antiquity, 15 tiles in Exploration, and 20 tiles in Modern, although impassable terrain such as Mountains or Natural Wonders may block routes if no alternate path exists, which makes the route requirement higher. Sea-based trade extends further, covering 30 tiles in Antiquity, 45 tiles in Exploration, and 60 tiles in Modern.
Tip: You can boost this trade range via Town Focus, Policies, or planting down more in-between Settlements.
Biomes, Features, and Terrain

Civilization VII features six biomes: Grassland, Plains, Desert, Marine, Tropical, and Tundra. Each biome has various features, including Floodplain, Forest, Ice, Lotus, Mangrove Swamp, Marsh, Natural Wonders, Oasis, Rainforest, Sagebrush Steppe, Savannah Woodland, Taiga, Tundra Bog, Watering Hole, Atoll, Aquatic, and Reef.
Meanwhile, terrain types include Flat, Rough, River, Mountainous, Coast, and Ocean. Yields on unworked tiles are determined by the combinatorics of biomes, features, and terrains.
Tip: While terrain and biomes provide some natural yields, more significant yields come from tile improvements that are unlocked and boosted by researching technology.
Rivers

In Civilization VII, rivers are drawn through the middle of hexes and come in two sizes: Navigable Rivers and Minor Rivers. All rivers affect land movement, but Navigable Rivers also support naval movement and specialized city buildings, such as Harbors and Shipyards. Navigable Rivers are a new terrain type, joining Flat, Rough, Mountain, Coast, and Ocean.

Navigable Rivers represent major real-world rivers like the Nile, Amazon, and Mississippi, which support significant shipping traffic. Land units can cross these rivers without the Sailing technology, and they support buildings with powerful bonuses, such as those requiring fresh water or water power.

Navigable Rivers allow for the construction of Bridges, allowing faster movement across them. They can flood, which damages tiles but also enhances their yields. Navigable Rivers can be occupied by both land and naval units, making them strategic arenas for both movement and combat. However, naval units fight at full strength on river tiles, so maintaining a strong naval presence can be crucial.
Tip: Navigable Rivers can boost an Empire by providing enhanced yields and supporting crucial buildings. Plan your settlements to maximize these benefits.
Lakes

Lakes in Civilization VII are treated as landlocked Marine tiles. While some may be connected to navigable rivers that lead to the ocean, lakes are discreet bodies of inland water. Land units must embark to enter lakes, and naval units can navigate as well as spawn in them if a Harbor Building is present. All lakes are counted as coastal marine for their surrounding land.

Bonuses around Lakes in-game reflect real-world societies that have established lakes as their lifeblood. The African and North American Great Lakes have fed their surrounding communities, while civilizations like that of the Baganda have created human-made lakes like Kabakas Lake as represented in Civilization VII.
Tip: If a Lake is not connected to Ocean Marine tiles, then there is no way to get the naval units spawned there into the open ocean. Construct your Harbor Buildings with care.
Ocean

The oceans that separate the swathes of land in Civilization VII are crucial for naval combat, resource improvement, and exploration. In the age of Antiquity, Marine Ocean tiles are typically restricted. While coastal movement is allowed, only specific Civilizations can traverse the deeper waters of the Marine biome. In the Exploration Age, units crossing the ocean are subject to rough seas, which end movement speed and deal damage every turn the unit spends in them. Researching the Shipbuilding Technology negates the effects of Rough Seas. In Modern, all Ocean terrain can be crossed without the danger of Rough Seas.
A majority of our real-world earth is water, contributing to vast oceans between continents. Goods as well as ideas make their way across the waters, bringing inspiration from far and wide.
Tip: Take caution on the Rough Seas! The damage dealt per turn can vary, so plan your routes accordingly.
Unit Types
Military Units
Military units can initiate combat and defend against attacks. These include infantry, ranged, Cavalry units, and more.
Support Units

Support units have no combat strength and can be attacked by military units without recourse. Support units offer exploration gameplay and other valuable interactions such as trade. Examples of support units include Settlers, Commanders, and Treasure Convoys.
Civilian Units
Civilian units cannot attack, and they cannot explore. They often have other specialized roles. Examples of Civilian Units include Merchants, Religious Units, Explorers, Prospectors and Migrants.
Tip: Protect your support and civilian units by keeping them close to military units. This ensures their safety and allows them to carry out their essential roles without disruption.
Stationed vs Garrisoned
Stationed Units
Military units located on top of an Urban district without walls are considered Stationed. These units are positioned within the district but do not receive additional defensive benefits.
Garrisoned Units

Military units stationed on top of a Walled Urban district are considered Garrisoned. These units benefit from enhanced defenses, as enemies must first destroy the Wall's HP defenses before they can attack the units stationed there.

Tip: Position your military units in Walled Urban districts to garrison them. This strategic placement enhances their defensive effectiveness, protecting your valuable urban areas from enemy assaults.
Army: Assembling

To Assemble an Army, select a Commander’s "Assemble" command, which consolidates surrounding units into a single stack. Alternatively, Units can be individually packed into a Commander. While Assembled, the Army moves as a single entity, allowing for streamlined travel across the map. If an Assembled Army is attacked, it defends as a single unit, leveraging the combined strength of all its components. Assembled Armies can initiate attacks and overrun weaker enemy units, but if an Army takes significant damage, it unpacks.
Tip: Use Assembling to quickly and efficiently move your Army across the map or flank the enemy backline.
Army: Reinforcement

Reinforcement streamlines moving units across the map. To use this operation, the unit must be a combat unit with full movement, undamaged, at least six tiles from a Commander, and in friendly territory. Each Commander can have at most four reinforcing units, but can reinforce while fully assembled. Land units cannot reinforce an embarked Army or cross the open ocean.

The selected unit travels with its base movement range while ignoring terrain modifiers. Upon arrival the unit will join the Commander's Army if there is available capacity, or enter a nearby tile if not.
Tip: Reinforcement is ideal for quickly bolstering your forces without micromanagement. However, remember that a reinforcement unit is unavailable during transit.
Army: Deploying

When Assembled, the Commander and all the units under them can move as a single unit. They can also add or remove units from the Army, overrun weaker enemies (requires 5:1 combat odds), and promote units within the formation.
When Deployed, the Commander can re-Assemble the units into a stacked formation, order ranged units to focus fire on a specific target, and coordinate melee units to attack simultaneously.
Tip: Use Overrun to clear weak enemies efficiently, but make sure to Deploy before a major battle. Utilize Focus Fire and Coordinated Attack to concentrate your offensive power on key targets.
Army: Fleets

Naval Fleets, commanded by a Fleet Commander, can Assemble into a single stack, Deploy into adjacent tiles, execute naval focus fire, and perform coastal bombardments. They can also escort packed Armies across bodies of water.
Tip: Use Fleet Commanders to escort units across the water and coordinate powerful coastal bombardments.
Army: Air Squadrons

Air Squadrons, commanded by a Squadron Commander, can Establish Air Bases on flat tiles with no Urban District that are not owned by another player. They can patrol to intercept enemy aircraft, conduct reconnaissance to reveal an area, execute carpet bombs, perform air strikes, rebase to nearby air bases, and airdrop infantry units to selected hexes.
Tip: Use Air Squadrons to gain strategic reconnaissance and provide rapid support to land operations with air strikes.
Pillaging

Both improvements and buildings can be pillaged. Once pillaged, their benefits vanish, and the unit that performed the pillaging receives a reward, or “plunder,” based on the structure it pillaged – these rewards, except for healing, increase in magnitude throughout the game.

Pillaging exhausts a Land Unit’s movement and allows one tile to be pillaged at a time. Naval Units can pillage multiple times a turn, referred to as Coastal Raiding. Urban tiles with two buildings must be pillaged one building at a time, starting with the highest-yield building. Once a building is pillaged, it cannot be pillaged again until it is repaired by its owner. Repairs can be completed through the Production Menu and require 25% of the building’s initial construction cost.
Tip: If you are locked in for a long war, use pillaging to heal your units and disrupt your opponent's economy and infrastructure to gain an advantage over time.
Ranged Combat

Ranged units do not suffer reciprocal damage when attacking, making them an excellent choice to pair with melee frontline units. However, ranged units are vulnerable to melee units, especially cavalry, which gain combat strength while attacking ranged units. Ranged units have a melee strength stat, which is used to calculate the damage they take when defending against melee attacks. However, ranged units’ melee strength is typically low.

Ranged Attacks provide the Combat Bonuses obtained during gameplay on the tile where your unit is currently positioned. This differs from Melee Attacks where bonuses apply on the defender’s tile where the attack takes place.
Tip: Damaged units lose some of their combat strength. The ability to attack without taking reciprocal damage is one of the greatest advantages of ranged combat.
Terrain Combat Modifier
In battle, the type of terrain can help or hurt your units. Each natural feature adds or subtracts a bonus to a unit’s defensive combat strength. Here’s a simple guide:

[BLIST][LI]Vegetated Areas: Forests, woodlands, and similar features give your units a +2 bonus in combat when defending.[LI]Wet Areas: Bogs, oasis, and other wet features lower your defensive combat strength by 2.[LI]Rough: If a tile is rough, it provides extra defense—currently a bonus of +3.[LI]Navigable Rivers: Naval units can sail on these without trouble. However, land units must embark (board a boat) to cross safely.[LI]Minor Rivers: These slow you down in combat. Attacking from a minor river tile gives your unit a penalty, and defending from one also makes your unit less effective.[/LIST]
Tip: Generally speaking, you would not want to defend on water tiles, while you’d get increased protection from standing on vegetated tiles and hills.
Air Combat

Air units fall into one of three categories: Fighters, Ground Attackers and Bombers. Fighters are strongest against other air units, Ground Attackers are strongest against Land and Sea units and Bombers are strongest against Fortifications.

Fighters have the unique ability to Intercept. When an enemy air unit attempts an action near a tile where Fighters are present one Fighter will automatically Intercept and attack the enemy unit and will receive a combat bonus for each additional Fighter packed with that Fighter.

Air units are always tied to a Commander: either an Aerodrome Commander, Squadron Commander or Aircraft Carrier. Air Units can use the Rebase action to move from one Commander to another that is within range, but cannot move on their own. Instead, their Movement determines the range of their actions. Air units cannot Rebase to a Squadron Commander until that Squadron Commander has used its Establish Air Base action. Air units cannot be built or purchased unless there are available slots on a Commander in that settlement.

Tip: Air units can attack while packed in a Commander by selecting them individually or all Air units of a single type can attack together by using the Commander's Focused Attack. Eligible targets for an attack will be highlighted on the map. Enemy units can only be attacked if they are visible but districts can be attacked as long as they have been explored.
Flanking

Once two units engage in combat, they are locked in a “front,” allowing additional attackers to strike from the sides or rear. Flanking bonuses scale by angle: front-left or front-right angles grant +2, back-left or back-right grant +3, and a direct rear attack provides +5. Certain civilizations, like the Mongols, can amplify these bonuses further (e.g., +50%).
Naval units can also flank, with naval melee units have a higher flanking bonus than their ranged counterparts.

Tip: Position multiple units to encircle foes from different angles, maximizing the flanking bonus and gaining a decisive combat edge. In Antiquity, you will need to research the Military Training technology to unlock the Flanking mechanic.
Intercept

Intercept is a PASSIVE ability that allows fighter-class units to engage enemy aircraft attempting to attack locations, units, or other targets within their intercept range, which is set to 3 tiles by default. Aerodrome extends this range by 1 for Fighters stationed inside, which provides a City better air protection. When an enemy aircraft initiates an attack within this range, it first engages in combat with the interceptor. Only if the attacking aircraft survives the interception does it proceed to strike its intended target.

Interceptors continue to intercept any incoming aircraft as long as they remain alive, providing sustained air defense coverage for nearby assets. This ability makes fighter units valuable for defending high-priority targets against enemy airstrikes.
Special Case for Nuclear Bombers: Bombers on nuclear missions are always successful in their drops, but if their health drops below 50, they will fail their nuke drop.

Tip: Place interceptors strategically to cover critical areas, ensuring they have overlapping ranges for maximum defense. Interceptors are essential for neutralizing enemy air threats and protecting ground forces and infrastructure from aerial assaults.
Fighter Sweep

A Fighter Sweep draws out and damages—or even destroys—enemy fighters, paving the way for a safer bombing run. By assigning your fighter units to a Squadron Commander, you can use the Sweep ability on a target location, forcing defending fighters to intercept. Once these hostile aircraft have been engaged or eliminated, your bombers can operate with far less risk.
Tip: Always perform a Fighter Sweep to reduce or eliminate enemy air defenses before sending in your bombers, especially your nuclear bombers.
Embark

When a unit embarks to traverse water tiles, it adopts a standardized combat strength that scales with the ages, rather than using its default land-based strength. Embarked units have 5 Combat Strength in the Antiquity Age, 25 Combat Strength in the Exploration Age, and 50 Combat Strength in the Modern Age. This means that, while they can defend themselves, they are generally more vulnerable compared to their strength on land.

A land unit's embarked movement speed is determined by Age – plus any bonus modifiers – and is independent from their normal land movement speed. The base embarked movement speed is 2 in Antiquity and 3 in later Ages.

Tip: Use Embark for quick water crossings, but avoid leaving units exposed on open water, as their reduced combat strength makes them susceptible to attacks. Prioritize Amphibious units for coastal operations if you need full combat strength on water.
Fortify

The Fortify action allows a unit to build temporary fortifications on its current tile, taking 2 turns to complete by default. Once fortifications are in place, the unit gains a +3 Combat Strength bonus when defending. This defensive bonus aligns with that of improvement fortifications like the Hillfort and Shore Battery, providing a solid defense boost against enemy attacks.

Tip: Use Fortify in strategic locations, especially in vulnerable areas or chokepoints, to strengthen your defense. Units in fortified positions can withstand attacks more effectively, making them valuable for holding critical territory.
Unit Abilities

Unit Abilities are special effects that can be applied to individual units or entire classes of units. You’ll know if a military unit has one of these abilities if it is listed in the combat preview that appears when you attempt an attack on an enemy unit. The following are examples:

Agile: Agility, for a fighter, can be the difference between returning victorious or in a casket. The Agile ability adds +1 Movement to the units it affects, giving them the speed to bring home the win. Tip: While vegetation and water still stop the movement of most units, those with the Agile ability may be able to run around such travel blockers.

Amphibious: The Amphibious ability allows a unit to ignore the usual Combat Strength penalty when attacking while Embarked, meaning that it uses its full default strength in combat against opponents. Additionally, units with Amphibious pay no additional movement cost to embark or disembark, allowing them to transition between land and water without losing mobility. Tip: Amphibious units are highly effective for coastal assaults and quick transitions between land and sea, enabling you to maintain full combat strength when attacking from water. Use them strategically to launch unexpected attacks and gain the upper hand in coastal engagements.

Caution in battle could save a life, but just as easily it could hinder an offensive strategy. The Cautious ability reflects a more diligent approach to battle, granting +3 Combat Strength when defending and inflicting -2 Combat Strength when attacking. Tip: Leave caution at home! Your Cautious units are best suited for defending from behind fortifications.

Cover: Duck and cover! Ranged units are less of a hassle when you have the Cover ability, which provides +2 Combat Strength against them. Tip: Facing off against ranged units requires speed and precision. Cover can give you the edge you need to break that line of archers.

Determined: Never give up, and never give in. The Determined ability gives units an additional +2 Combat Strength in all situations. Tip: Might is right! The higher a unit’s Combat Strength, the more damage they deal.

Dispirited: Lack of funds, rations, or competent leadership can lead to a decline in morale amongst troops. The Dispirited ability subtracts -2 Combat Strength in all situations. Tip: Units are most likely to become Dispirited during Narrative Events, so make sure to choose the option that supports the story you want to tell.

Poison: Units that possess the Poison ability are masters of the toxic arts, gaining additional Combat Strength when they attack or defend against those with less than 100% Health. Tip: Using a unit with the Poison ability can be devastating when timed correctly. Attack with other units first, then use your Poison unit's +5 Combat Strength against the wounded.

Reckless: The best defense is a good offense. When units are riled up under the effect of the Reckless ability, they receive +3 Combat Strength when attacking, but -2 Combat Strength when defending. Strike true in your attacks, because your defensive capabilities have taken a hit with the unit’s hotheaded nature. Tip: Use units with the Reckless ability when sacking cities. Those fortifications won’t stand a chance against your extra firepower.

Skirmish: Using sheer numbers to overwhelm an enemy's forces is a tried-and-true strategy. It is even more effective when utilizing units with the Skirmish ability, which adds +50% Combat Strength from flanking the enemy with multiple units. Tip: Use units possessing the Skirmish ability when flanking to deal as much damage as possible.

Sluggish: Battle can take a toll on both body and spirit. Units with the Sluggish ability have been worn down by the horrors of battle, and take a -1 Movement penalty. Tip: Units are most likely to become Sluggish during Narrative Events, so make sure to choose the option that supports the story you want to tell.

Splash: When attacking with a Unit that has the Splash ability, enemy Units in tiles adjacent to the target tile will also take 25% damage. Tip: The Splash ability is great for big, stubborn groups of enemies. Use its damage on enemy units adjacent to the target to break up tightly-formed blockades.

Stealth: Stealth units are invisible to all enemy units by default. A Stealth unit only becomes visible when it attacks an enemy unit, it ends its turn adjacent to an enemy unit, or an enemy unit enters its location. Tip: Aside from surprise combat, try using Stealth units to keep an eye on other Civs. Watching foreign Wonder building progress, scouting target Military formations, and more can better inform your next move.

Swift: Fast as the wind, units with the Swift ability ignore the Zone of Control exerted by enemy units. This means they can move freely in spite of the presence of enemies on the battlefield, and their movement is not stopped by entering a Zone of Control. Tip: A unit with the Swift ability can escape from deadly combat scenarios with ease. It's not a retreat – it's a backwards advance!
Coastal Raiding

The style of pillaging that Naval Units can perform is a Coastal Raid, and it can be performed multiple times a turn. This pillages and captures the adjacent selected tile if able, as well as rewards the raiding unit by repairing damage and yielding gold.
Tip: Coastal Raiding can also trigger adjacent discoveries, giving the action a boon outside of combat situations.
Technologies

Technologies represent new scientific advancements or inventions for your civilization. Each researched technology unlocks new buildings, units, and other advancements, enhancing the power and capabilities of an empire.
Technologies are developed through a continuous research process, driven by the Science yield.
Selecting a Tech or Civic deeper in the tree will queue up the pre-requisite nodes for you automatically.
Tip: Focusing on technology research is an excellent way to gain a military advantage, as most military units are locked behind technologies.
Civics

Civics are similar to Technologies in that they are also researched; however they use the Culture yield to progress. Civics can unlock Wonders, Units, and Buildings. Unlike Technologies, Civics often provide Policies that can be slotted into a Government.
Selecting a Tech or Civic deeper in the tree will queue up the pre-requisite nodes for you automatically.
Tip: While Civics unlock Policies that can be slotted, Happiness ultimately grants extra slots. Maintain a balanced focus on both!
Masteries

Both Techs and Civics offer players opportunities to research Masteries. After a Tech or Civic is researched, a tier two Tech or Civic sometimes become available. These are called Masteries, and they grant additional bonuses that unlock new constructibles and codices.

Tip: Masteries are often essential for both the Science and Culture Victories. Several Triumphs also require completing Tech and Civic Masteries. Prioritize them to strengthen your civilization’s focus in these areas.
Towns and Economy

Towns automatically convert their production into Gold income, making them a crucial part of your economy. Expansion leads to additional income, but this comes with increased risk as you might anger neighboring Leaders and Independents.
Tip: Expanding your towns boosts your economy, but be mindful that you don’t exceed the Settlement cap.
Fresh Water

Establishing a Settlement on Fresh Water, identified by blue tiles in the Settler Lens, grants a permanent +5 Happiness bonus. You can toggle the Settler Lens via the icon above the minimap to spot these ideal locations.

Tip: Settle on Fresh Water whenever possible to maintain higher Happiness and reduce Unhappiness in your Settlements. An Unhappy Settlement takes a penalty to all of its yields, with each point of negative Happiness causing a 5% overall reduction.
Appeal

Land tiles near mountains, coasts, [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_NAVIGABLE_RIVER_TOOLTIP]Navigable Rivers[/TIP], and [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_NATURAL_WONDER_TOOLTIP]Natural Wonders[/TIP] have Appeal. Higher Appeal, from Average to Breathtaking, increases the Happiness of improved rural tiles.

Land tiles adjacent to items of natural beauty (forests, savannah woodlands, sagebrush steppe, mangrove swamp, taiga, mountains, coasts, navigable rivers, and natural wonders) have an "appealing" quality that influences the Happiness yield available from that tile. A tile's Appeal score can be Average, Charming, or Breathtaking based on the number of items of natural beauty around it. Each adjacent item of natural beauty grants +1 Appeal, with 3 being the threshold for Charming, and 5 for Breathtaking. Charming rural tiles with an improvement receive +1 Happiness, while an improved Breathtaking rural tile receives +2 Happiness. Natural Wonders are also tiles of great natural beauty, but their yields are unique to each wonder and therefore do not always include Happiness.
Tip: Some buildings can receive an adjacency bonus from Appealing tiles. Using Buildings and Improvements to maximize on the Appeal of tiles can boost the Happiness of your empire.
Migrant Gameplay
Migrants are special units that are created via various Narrative Events, Wonder effects, and when a Settlement runs out of space to grow.

When a Settlement runs out of Rural tiles to improve and has no available Specialist slots, a migrant will appear instead of a growth event. That Settlements required Food to grow will still increase as usual. You can activate a migrant in any Settlement that still has open Rural tiles, adding a Population to improve an available Rural tile.
Tip: You need to walk your Migrants to a Settlement before activating them. Once activated, they cannot be taken out again.
Unrest
When you capture a Settlement, it falls into unrest for several turns, causing unhappiness and stopping it from building or buying anything. Any captured Settlement also downgrades into a Town.

Placing a commander in the Settlement will help lower this unhappiness. If you conquer a Settlement that originally belonged to you, all unrest penalties disappear because the city is considered liberated.
Tip: Gaining Settlements through peace deals avoids unrest, so sometimes it's smart to mix diplomacy with your military actions.
Urban Population

Urban Population counts only the citizens generated by constructing buildings—it does not include Specialists. Some effects may care about the number of Urban Population in a settlement. Here are a couple of examples:
[BLIST][LI]Abbasid's Mamluk: +1 Combat Strength for every Urban Population.[LI]Inca Tradition: Settlements receive +0.5 Gold for every Urban Population.[/LIST]
Tip: Focus on constructing buildings to boost your Urban Population when playing Civs that benefit from it.
Starvation

Starvation is uncommon in Civilization VII, thanks to the new approach to managing Food. Unlike previous games, only Specialists require Food upkeep—regular Rural and Urban populations do not. However, starvation can still occur under specific conditions, such as having too many Specialists or when your Settlement suffers from very low Happiness.

If your Settlement’s net Food output turns negative, starvation may begin to set in. When starvation fully sets in, it will harm your Settlement by lowering Happiness and destroying one of its buildings or improvements. Always keep an eye on your Food supply and Settlement Happiness to avoid the consequences of starvation.

Tip: If your City is starving, consider specializing a connected Town to help feed it. If low Happiness is the issue, stationing a high-level Commander in the City can significantly reduce the Unhappiness it generates.
Land and Territory

[BLIST][LI]Owned Tile: A tile within your Settlement’s borders.[LI]Unowned Tile: A tile that is not yet part of any Settlement’s borders.[LI]Improved Tile: A Rural tile with an improvement (worked by a population point).[LI]Unimproved Tile: A Rural tile without an improvement (no population assigned to it).[LI]Friendly Tile: A tile you own, or owned by your allied Civs and City-States.[LI]Neutral Tile: A tile not owned by any Civilization.[LI]Enemy Tile: A tile owned by a Civilization you are at war with.[/LIST]
Tip: A lot of effects function according to these tile types. Make sure to check what type of tile a specific effect mentions when making a decision.
Merchants

Merchants can travel to other leaders’ settlements to establish trade routes, gaining access to their resources. Merchants are also useful in building roads within an empire. Make sure to research the corresponding tech/civic to unlock Merchants again after every Age Transition.

In Antiquity and Exploration Age, your Merchants must first move into other Civilizations' borders, before being able to use the create trade route function. There's no such limitation in the Modern Age.

Tip: Merchants are your primary method for acquiring foreign resources. Use them strategically to strengthen your economy and complete certain Triumphs. Additionally, you can use Merchants to build roads within your Empire, which can help you connect Towns to Cities in order to feed them.
Settlement Limit

Settlement Limit represents the size of empire, in total Settlements, that you can govern without consequences. This limit is a soft cap and can be exceeded by settling or conquering additional Settlements. Each Settlement you control over your Settlement Limit incurs a -5 Happiness penalty in each of your Settlements, per Settlement over the limit. There is no cap to this penalty, so an over-extended empire can suffer severe consequences for greedy expansion. The Settlement Limit can be increased via the Tech, Civic, and Attribute trees.
Razed Settlements do not count toward the limit once completed Razed. However, they incur other penalties.
Tip: Staying under the Settlement Limit can help maintain a Happy and stable empire.
City Limit
A City Limit represents the number of Cities that you can govern without consequences. This limit is a hard cap associated with certain unique Civilizations.
Tip: Civilizations that have a hard City Limit, like Carthage having a limit of 1, cannot convert Towns to Cities when the cap is fulfilled.
Razing

When a Settlement is captured, the capturer can choose to raze it. Razing a Settlement requires multiple turns to accomplish, and the number of turns correlates to the size (population) of the Settlement. Tiles are razed from the farthest tiles to center.
Razing incurs a -2 influence per age penalty for rest of the age.
Once the process of Razing has started, it cannot be stopped whatsoever. Once a player starts to raze a settlement it cannot be stopped by that player, regardless of diplomatic status.
Tip: Razing is an effective way to stay under the Settlement cap if you decide to go Warmongering. However, be wary of its negative consequences.
Burning Status

Some attacks or effects inflict a Burning status on a tile, dealing a flat 15 damage per turn to any unit standing there. This damage is unaffected by either the attacker’s or defender’s combat strength, and the duration depends on the specific source. For instance, the Burning Arrow unit states a two-turn duration in its description.
Tip: Move units off burning tiles quickly to avoid taking significant damage over multiple turns.
Specialist

Assigning Population to an Urban tile creates a Specialist. Specialists amplify the tile's adjacency bonuses and provide additional Yield based on the adjacencies of all of the Buildings in that Urban District. However, they come with a trade-off, requiring -2 Food and Happiness per Age in Maintenance on current Age Buildings, and -1 Food and Happiness (not per Age) Maintenance on Warehouse Buildings and Obsolete Buildings.
While Towns can acquire Urban tiles by purchasing buildings, only Cities have the ability to gain Specialists, making them a key part of tall, City-focused play.

Tip: Strategically place Specialists in high-adjacency Urban tiles to maximize Yields. Keep an eye on Food and Happiness, as Specialists can strain resources in rapidly growing Cities, potentially causing negative Happiness and starvation.
Ocean Exploration

In Civilization VII, ocean movement varies depending on the type of water tile. Dark blue tiles represent open ocean and function similarly to rough land tiles, consuming all movement points and ending a unit's action until Shipbuilding is researched. Light blue tiles indicate coastal waters, which act like flat land tiles. Units in coastal waters can move and heal using their full movement points.

Units ending their turn on open ocean tiles will take damage due to ocean attrition unless Shipbuilding has been researched. This mechanic adds an element of risk to early ocean exploration, making technological advancements essential for safe passage.
On higher difficulty levels, AI civilizations suffer less damage from ocean attrition, making them more resilient during early exploration.
Research Cartography early to allow your Settlers to cross the ocean. However, your Cog unit can explore the ocean as early as turn 1 of the Exploration Age.
Roads

Roads are automatically created between nearby settlements upon their establishment, allowing for efficient unit movement. Merchants can also be deployed to manually build roads. When a Town is connected to a City via roads, it can support the City by feeding it once it specializes, enhancing the City's growth.
Tip: Use Merchants strategically to establish road connections between key settlements, especially if the automatic road network is insufficient. This will enable better urban growth.
Railroad
Railroads provide fast travel between settlements in Civilization VII, enhancing logistical efficiency across your empire.

To build a railroad, ensure that two settlements are connected by roads and that each has its own Rail Station, as well as the Capital. Once both Rail Stations are built, the railroad connection is established, allowing for rapid movement between the connected settlements.

Once the Capital has a Rail Network established, units positioned on or adjacent to a Rail Station can travel to another Rail Station within 20 tiles in a single turn. This travel consumes all of the unit's movement points for that turn, but it allows for quick relocation across your empire, significantly boosting strategic flexibility.
Strategically place Rail Stations in key settlements to create an efficient transportation network, allowing your units to quickly respond to threats or reinforce distant regions.
Tip: To connect a large empire, you will likely need to build Ports. Ports can connect Rail Stations that are split by water.
Religion Overview

Pantheon plays the role of proto-religion the Antiquity Age, players unlock their first Pantheon by researching the Mysticism civic. Pantheons provide unique bonuses often related to natural features and lay the foundation for religious gameplay. Constructing an Altar enables players to benefit from their Pantheon.

Religion becomes available in the Exploration Age. You can start a Religion by completing the Piety Civic and building a Temple. It provides various Belief types:[BLIST][LI]Enhancer: the Enhancer Belief aids in spreading the player’s religion. Each player may have only one Enhancer Belief.[LI]Reliquary: this Belief type allows players to earn Relics, which can be displayed for bonuses. Players may have only one Reliquary Belief.[LI]Founder: awarded initially upon founding a religion, with two additional Founder Beliefs awarded later, for a maximum of three. Founder Beliefs offer yields and other benefits for converting foreign settlements, incentivizing active religious spread.[/LIST]
A Holy City is the birthplace of a player's religion. This city serves as a stronghold for the player’s chosen faith.
Converting most settlements to your religion requires 2 Missionary charges. However, if the settlement has zero rural population or is being converted for the first time, only 1 charge is needed.
Tip: Focus on settlements with no existing religious influence to maximize your Missionary charges and establish a strong religious presence early.
Religious Gameplay

Missionaries only spread their founder’s religion, and opponents’ Holy Cities CAN be converted to your religion. Independent Peoples cannot adopt a religion until they become City-States. Additional Founder Beliefs are extremely rare and often triggered by random events. There are two Religion flags on the City banner of each Settlement affected by Religion. Both flags need to match, in order for the Settlement to be considered as converted. One flag represents Urban religion, while the other flag represents Rural religion.

Tip: Being the first to spread Religion to a Settlement converts both flags at the same time. If a Settlement already has a Religion, you will need to convert an Urban tile and a Rural tile to accomplish the conversion.
Ideologies

Emerging in Modern, new Ideologies come forth with new ideas on how to run an empire. Studying the Political Theory Civic will unlock the ability to study an Ideology Civic. This choice cannot be changed later, as you must pick between the three Ideologies--Communism, Democracy, and Fascism. Once selected, further Civics are available for study based on the player's Ideology.

When an Ideology is selected by a player, all other players with an Ideology will gain a Relationship change based on that selection. If players share an Ideology, they will receive a positive Relationship increase. If players adopt opposing Ideologies, they will receive a negative Relationship decrease.
Tip: Certain Ideologies support certain yield types best. Generally, Communism focuses on Food and Science, Democracy focuses on Culture and Happiness, and Fascism focuses on Gold and Production.
Bankruptcy

If your gold income is negative, you risk bankruptcy. When the treasury balance falls below zero while your income is negative, units with the highest maintenance costs will disband one by one until the balance is restored. This can severely impact military and economic stability, so maintaining a positive income is essential.
Tip: Keep an eye on maintenance costs when expanding your military or building new structures. Avoiding bankruptcy is crucial for sustained growth and security.
Connected Settlements

Connected Settlements facilitate resource and food management between Cities and Towns. There are two types of connections:[BLIST][LI]Trade Connections: Settlements within trade range can freely move resources between them. This connection is ideal for distributing resources across the empire.[LI]Road and Sea Connections: Settlements are linked directly by roads or are both coastal and on the same continent. Towns connected to Cities this way can feed those Cities when selecting a Town Focus.[/LIST]
Tip: Establish trade and road connections early to optimize resource movement and enable Towns to support City growth.
Pirating

Some Units have the [icon:UNIT_CAUTION] Pirate ability, or gain it from a Civilization or Leader ability. Units that have the [icon:UNIT_CAUTION] Pirate ability can cross the borders of other civilizations, plunder trade routes from non-Allied civilizations, and attack Units of non-Allied Civilizations without Declaring War. Defeating units reduces relationship with the civilization or Independent Power. Non-Allied Civilizations can also attack these units, and they remain in hostile borders after Declaring War. Defeating Pirate Units will not reduce relationship with that Civilization. Privateering is counted as pirating, and any privateer ship is subject to pirating rules.
Tip: Try keeping your Units in Fortified Districts. This will allow you to attack Pirates, but the District defenses will protect you from being attacked.
Just One More Turn

Just One More Turn mode allows you to continue your game beyond victory, giving you the freedom to keep exploring, building, and shaping the world even after your story officially concludes. Whether you want to admire your accomplishments, further develop your empire, or simply enjoy the gameplay without pressure, Just One More Turn lets you extend the experience at your leisure.
After you reach the end of the final age, you'll see the "Just One More Turn" option alongside your victory summary. Selecting it keeps your game running, allowing you to resume play right away.
In this mode, you've already won, so additional victories won't end your game, though you can still complete Triumphs and enjoy their rewards and achievements.

Tip: You'll always know you're in Just One More Turn mode thanks to a persistent reminder at the top left of your screen. When you're finally ready to conclude your adventure, simply exit to the main menu. There's always one more turn waiting for you if you want it!
Force-Ending Turns (PC-Only)

By pressing Shift + Enter on PC, you can ignore all turn-blocking notifications and immediately end your turn. Please keep in mind that this practice is mostly used when you are stuck, and it’s often controversial in multiplayer due to potential exploits.
Tip: Avoid using this mechanic if playing competitively.
Team Play
In Multiplayer, players can form teams. To set this up, players should select the same team in the team dropdown menu when creating a multiplayer game.

When playing on a team, teammates are locked into an Alliance that cannot be broken and are locked at the max Relationship level. Unlike a standard Alliance, teammates share map visibility. Teammates may use Diplomatic Actions with one another but are prohibited from using Espionage Actions.

Teammates share a Relationship status, and a War and Alliance status, with all other players and teams. When negotiating peace, one player from each team will manage the negotiations. Once a deal is reached, all other players on each team will make peace automatically with no further exchanges.
If one player on a team achieves a Victory, all teammates share in the Victory. If there is a Score Victory, the team with the highest score wins.
Note: Technology and Civic progress, Triumph progress, and Victory progress is [B]not[/B] shared between teammates.
Legends System

The [B]Legends[/B] system is Civilization VII's meta-progression framework, tracking your accomplishments across all your games. It recognizes your feats and turns your cumulative successes into lasting rewards. Through this system, each game adds to your achievements, unlocking both cosmetic customizations and gameplay-enhancing items known as [B]Mementos[/B].

Legends consist of four interconnected parts: Legend Challenges, Legend Paths, Legend XP, and Mementos. Together, they ensure that every game matters, encouraging diverse strategies and rewarding consistent play. Whether you win, lose, or try something entirely new, you steadily build toward something bigger than any single match.

Tip: Treat Legends as a rewarding extra layer rather than a mandatory system. Play your way, experiment freely, and you'll naturally find yourself unlocking bonuses and enhancing your civilization’s long-term capabilities.
Legends XP

Legend XP is the currency that drives progression within the Legends system, gained exclusively by completing Legend Challenges. Each completed challenge awards a certain amount of XP toward its corresponding Legend Path: Foundation Challenges reward XP for your global Foundation Path, while Leader Challenges boost specific Leader Paths.

The amount of XP earned depends on a challenge's complexity. Crucially, this XP accumulates even if you lose the game, meaning every match contributes to your overall Legends progression, win or lose. There's no shortcut—only gameplay accomplishments earn Legend XP, making each achievement feel valuable.
Tip: Don’t abandon tough matches early. Completing a few extra challenges can still provide valuable Legend XP, making your efforts worthwhile even in defeat.
Legend Challenges

Legend Challenges are special objectives you can complete while playing Civilization VII. These tasks act like quests or achievements, offering clear goals that range from simple feats like constructing your first Wonder to ambitious achievements such as dominating a victory type. Challenges come in two forms: Foundation Challenges, which can be completed with any leader, and Leader Challenges, unique to specific leaders and their abilities.

Whenever you fulfill the conditions of a challenge, you immediately earn Legend XP. This XP advances your Legend Paths, making each completed challenge meaningful—even if your current match isn’t going well. You can easily track your ongoing and completed challenges through the Challenge Log, helping you target goals aligned with your strategy.
Tip: Regularly check your Challenges Log. Completing even a few objectives can turn a losing game into progress for your long-term Legend growth.
Legend Paths
Basics

Legend Paths represent your overall advancement within Civilization VII's Legends system. They function like experience tracks, leveling up as you earn Legend XP by completing Legend Challenges. There are two main types: the universal [B]Foundation Path[/B] and specialized [B]Leader Paths[/B] specific to each leader.
Balance your efforts between different paths to maximize your long-term benefits. The Foundation Path offers broad rewards, while Leader Paths grant specialized advantages.
Foundation Path

The Foundation Path tracks your progress across all your games, regardless of leader choice. It has 50 levels, each unlocking various rewards, such as cosmetic profile upgrades (badges, banners, titles) and powerful gameplay bonuses called [B]Mementos[/B]. Importantly, leveling this path also unlocks [B]Memento Slots[/B], essential for equipping these bonuses.
Prioritize early levels in your Foundation Path to quickly unlock your first Memento Slots, significantly enhancing your gameplay options.
Leader Path

Each leader in Civilization VII has their own unique Leader Path, which levels up through Leader Challenges specific to their abilities and history. Leader Paths go up to level 10, offering leader-themed Mementos, cosmetic items, and special gameplay advantages tailored to their playstyle.

Tip: Experiment with different leaders regularly to unlock a diverse set of Leader Path rewards. Mementoes unlocked for one leader can be used with any other leaders as well. Pairing specialized mementoes with their respective leaders can often unlock powerful synergies.
Mementos
Basics
Mementos are special items earned from your Legends progression, which can be equipped before each game to provide unique in-game bonuses.
They function like gear for your leader, giving effects ranging from basic stat boosts to situational advantages. Every leader can equip up to two Mementos, offering powerful strategic flexibility.

Carefully choose your Mementos before starting a game, matching them to your desired victory type or compensating for your leader's weaknesses. [B]Keep in mind that Mementos can also be swapped between Ages.[/B]
Unlocking and Collection

You unlock Mementos by reaching specific milestones within your Legend Paths. Some Mementos come from higher Foundation Path levels, while many are leader-specific rewards earned by progressing through Leader Paths. Once unlocked, they permanently join your collection and can be freely equipped by any leader.
Unlocking a variety of Mementos by playing multiple leaders can significantly broaden your strategic options, even if you later return to your favorite leader.
Strategies and Synergies

The variety of nearly 100 unique Mementos allows for extensive strategic combinations. Some offer straightforward bonuses, such as extra Economic or Cultural points at game start, while others trigger situationally, like spawning free units after successful espionage actions. Cleverly combining Mementos can lead to powerful or unique strategies, amplifying your strengths or mitigating weaknesses.
Tip: Experiment with different Memento combinations to discover powerful synergies. An unexpected pairing might provide just the advantage you need for your chosen victory path.
